analysis.one_liner: Bars the EPA from spending any money to limit greenhouse gas pollution from power plants and factories.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it died in a House subcommittee after being referred there in February 2013.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have prohibited any federal money from being used by the Environmental Protection Agency to run a cap-and-trade program or to enforce any new rule limiting greenhouse gas emissions — carbon dioxide, methane, and others — from stationary sources like power plants and factories, including rules under the Clean Air Act. In effect, it would have blocked the EPA from writing or enforcing any new limits on industrial greenhouse gas pollution. It was referred to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Energy and Power Subcommittee, where it sat until the 113th Congress ended without any vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Power plants, factories, and other industrial facilities that burn fossil fuels would be spared any new EPA limits on their greenhouse gas emissions, including new permitting requirements. Coal-heavy utilities and fossil fuel producers would avoid compliance costs from any future cap-and-trade or emissions rules.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Fossil-fuel power plants and industrial emitters

how_it_helps.text: The bill would cut off all EPA funding for implementing or enforcing a cap-and-trade program — a system where the government issues a limited number of permits to emit greenhouse gases — for any program established after enactment.

It would also block EPA funding for any new statutory or regulatory requirement on greenhouse gas emissions from stationary sources, including rules under Clean Air Act section 111 (the basis for power-plant emissions standards) and Clean Air Act permitting requirements.

The bill defines greenhouse gas broadly, covering carbon dioxide, methane, nitrous oxide, sulfur hexafluoride, hydrofluorocarbons, perfluorocarbons, and any other designated gas, so the funding ban would reach essentially all EPA greenhouse-gas rules for industrial sources.

analysis.who_pays: The costs of greenhouse gas pollution — air quality impacts near industrial facilities and the risks of a warming climate — would fall on the public, with no EPA pathway to limit emissions from power plants and factories for as long as the funding ban was in force. The agency would also lose its ability to respond to any new emissions problem from stationary sources.
analysis.who_pays_short: Everyone breathing the air and bearing climate costs

drawbacks.text: The bill would leave the EPA unable to set or enforce any new limits on greenhouse gas pollution from power plants and factories — including rules under Clean Air Act section 111 — indefinitely, removing the main tool the federal government had for limiting industrial carbon emissions.

Supporters argued that EPA greenhouse gas rules raise energy prices and impose compliance costs on utilities and manufacturers; an honest account must note that blocking the rules shifts those costs off industry and onto public health and climate outcomes instead.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered a real, one-sided trade: it would spare fossil-fuel facilities compliance costs but would strip the EPA of funding to regulate any new greenhouse gas emissions from stationary sources, leaving the public to absorb the health and climate consequences with no federal check. Its titles aside, it was not a balanced energy policy but a blanket defunding of greenhouse gas regulation. It never advanced far enough for that trade to be tested in a vote.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Energy and Commerce Committee and then to its Energy and Power Subcommittee in February 2013, and no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever happened before Congress ended in January 2015.

narrative.text: Rep. Ted Poe introduced the bill on February 12, 2013, joined by 34 Republican cosponsors and no Democrats.
The House referred it to the Energy and Commerce Committee on the day of introduction, and on February 15, 2013 it was referred to the Subcommittee on Energy and Power.
No further action appears in the record; the bill never received a committee vote or a floor vote before the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: The public's existing protections were the default: because the bill died, the EPA kept the legal ability to write and enforce greenhouse gas limits for power plants and factories, while the fossil-fuel facilities that would have gained a shield never got one.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: The public; EPA's authority stayed intact

for.name: Rep. Ted Poe
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill to bar EPA funding for cap-and-trade and new greenhouse gas rules for stationary sources.

for.name: 34 House Republicans
for.what_they_did: Signed on as cosponsors of the bill.

against.name: House Energy and Commerce Committee
against.role: Committee of referral; never scheduled a hearing or markup
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral and its Energy and Power Subcommittee held it; no hearing, markup, or vote ever took place.

sides.party_line_note: All 35 sponsors and cosponsors were Republicans with no Democratic support, but the bill never reached a vote, so no one ever had to go on record for or against it.

industries.industry: Coal- and gas-fired electric utilities and other stationary-source emitters
industries.note: The bill would have barred the EPA from enforcing any new greenhouse gas limits or permitting requirements on their plants, sparing them compliance costs while the public absorbed the pollution and climate consequences.

industries.industry: Coal producers and fossil fuel extraction
industries.note: Blocking a cap-and-trade program and new emissions rules would preserve demand for coal and other fossil fuels by keeping carbon costs off their products.
